look_here_first: FIRST check the WAXY UPPER leaf surface and underside's small regular near-isodiametric vein areoles using reflected light / 10×, then the 5–12+ leafy bracts on each flowering peduncle. Willowleaf aster has stiffer, progressively reduced leaves and an ample densely leafy panicle. This sharply strengthens the split from S. lanceolatum, which generally has 1–3(–5) peduncle bracts and a less-waxy adaxial blade.

project_inclusion.learner_admission_basis: Existing reviewed B120 source-pool learner draft; range hold is not an admission veto
project_inclusion.range_basis: B120 review verified Travis PRC specimen; a historical Berlandier route between Bexar and upper Guadalupe is not assignable to a modern county. No three-county target-zone proof.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Never count as confirmed target-zone native until independent county-range evidence resolves the hold; selected images are Ontario comparison material.

best_field_traits: Tall rhizomatous perennial often in colonies.
Narrow lance-shaped, willow-like leaves on ascending stems; compare basal versus upper leaves.
Stems may show longitudinal hair lines and reddish coloration; confirm with hand lens.
Check peduncle, phyllary series, and cypsela/pappus to exclude other tall asters.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Versus S. lanceolatum (including nominate subspecies): praealtum tends to have stiff progressively reduced stem leaves, a waxy adaxial face, regular small/isodiametric areoles on abaxial face, and 5–12+ foliage-like peduncle bracts; lanceolatum usually has pliable, not waxy leaves with irregular/less marked underside areoles and 1–3(–5) peduncle bracts. Measured involucre characters overlap; keep taxon and range HOLD if evidence inadequate.
